{"id": "93:7/q03", "question": "What state does 'He found you ḍāllan' describe?", "turns_on": "Whether it describes missing revealed knowledge, searching, prior religious error, his people, obscurity, literal loss, or a specific unmet need.", "positions": [{"id": "93:7/q03/p1", "position": "He did not yet know revelation, prophetic signs, or religious law, and God taught him.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj and many later authors cite 42:52; others cite 12:3, 2:282, and 26:20. Al-Bayḍāwī and al-Biqāʿī add inspiration and sound reasoning; Bursawī says reason alone cannot discover these rulings. Al-Biqāʿī calls lack of guidance the effect of lacking a teacher. Al-Ṭabrisī links teaching seekers in 93:10 to this favor."}, {"id": "93:7/q03/p2", "position": "He lost the road on a Syrian caravan journey with Abū Ṭālib and was returned.", "reasons": "Some reports say Satan diverted the camel and Gabriel blew him to Abyssinia or India; others say a disbeliever held the reins or simply that the road was lost. Maysara is mentioned by some as Khadīja's servant. Jishumī conditions his explanation on the report's soundness."}, {"id": "93:7/q03/p3", "position": "He was literally lost as a child in Mecca's ravines and returned to his grandfather.", "reasons": "Accounts variously name Abū Jahl, an enemy, as the rescuer; some mention sheep, a grandfather praying, hunger, a camel that would only move with Muhammad in front, and comparison with Moses preserved through an enemy. Ibn ʿAbbās is the common attribution. Al-Qushayrī transmits a different rescuer, the uncle Abū Ṭālib, in a Meccan-passes account."}, {"id": "93:7/q03/p4", "position": "Ḥalīma lost the child near Mecca after weaning, and he was recovered under a tree.", "reasons": "Kaʿb's long version has an old man consult Hubal; idols fall and foretell the child's overthrow of them; ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib prays and a heavenly voice points to a tree in Tihāma. Later summaries vary the location between gate, road, and valley."}, {"id": "93:7/q03/p5", "position": "The astray ones were his people; God guided them through him.", "reasons": "The addressee may stand for his people. Abū Ḥayyān parses an omitted possessive as in 'ask the town' (12:82); al-Ālūsī dismisses his dream presentation, and Bint al-Shāṭiʾ says the ellipsis is unnecessary. Al-Ḥasan's explanatory readings express guidance through the Prophet, though the transmitted verbal form varies."}, {"id": "93:7/q03/p6", "position": "He was hidden, unknown, or unrecognized among his people until God made him and his worth known.", "reasons": "Al-Tirmidhī and ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Yaḥyā emphasize public recognition. Al-Rāzī likens concealment to water submerged in milk; al-Sulamī describes hidden prophethood and divine favors becoming manifest. Some say Muslims were guided to recognize him."}, {"id": "93:7/q03/p7", "position": "He was amid misguided people, and God guided him away from their error to monotheism and prophethood.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ, al-Kalbī, Ibn ʿAbbās, and others take the preposition 'among' as implied. Some reports say he seemed one of them, or that God rescued him from their misguidance, while declining to say he held it."}, {"id": "93:7/q03/p8", "position": "He had followed his people's way or religion for forty years before guidance.", "reasons": "Al-Suddī's forty years recur in al-Ṭabarī and later sources; al-Zajjāj reports a group saying so. Sources differ whether 'way' means customary life or unbelief. Al-Qurṭubī limits the claim to outward customs without idolatry; Ibn ʿAṭiyya names customs he shared and others he opposed, including the report from Zayd ibn ʿAmr."}, {"id": "93:7/q03/p9", "position": "He was in love or desired guidance, and God led him to the beloved or to service of God.", "reasons": "Versions differ: love for Abū Ṭālib redirected to God, already loving God, loving guidance, or longing for gnosis. Al-Rāzī cites Jacob's love (12:95) and says law enabled service of the Beloved."}, {"id": "93:7/q03/p10", "position": "He had been an unbeliever or astray from religious truth before God guided him.", "reasons": "The reported literal reading invokes 42:52, 12:3, 39:65 and 28:86; Mujāhid says he lacked guidance to his religion. Al-Kalbī is reported variously as finding him an unbeliever among an unbelieving people or guiding him from their error to monotheism. The Study Quran reports the literal reading."}, {"id": "93:7/q03/p11", "position": "He lacked knowledge of the particular prophethood and future rank appointed for him.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī and al-Thaʿlabī describe a state unlike his later one; al-Māwardī specifies absence of prophethood. Al-Rāzī says neither he nor Jews and Christians expected a prophet outside Israel. Al-Qurṭubī calls the state unawareness of what prophethood would mean for him."}, {"id": "93:7/q03/p12", "position": "He was perplexed and seeking the right way before revelation, while rejecting the surrounding religions.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya says he followed no one's creed but searched and reflected; Ibn ʿĀshūr says God inspired rejection of polytheism to prepare him. Elmalılı says pagan, Jewish, and Christian practices did not disclose the true law. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ and Islahi cite 42:52 and 12:3; Islahi places the search at Ḥirāʾ and compares Ḥanīf seekers. Qutb says revelation resolved confusion."}, {"id": "93:7/q03/p13", "position": "He was confused about explaining the revealed Book, and God taught him its explanation.", "reasons": "Al-Junayd and others cite 16:44 and 16:64; al-Ālūsī calls this close to the main explanation."}, {"id": "93:7/q03/p14", "position": "He sought the qibla, uncertain whether the Kaʿba would be granted, and God directed him there.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī derives 'seeking' from a lost person's search; al-Rāzī and al-Qurṭubī cite 2:144 and the Prophet turning his face heavenward."}, {"id": "93:7/q03/p15", "position": "He stood uniquely amid a barren religious setting, like a lone tree by which others find their way.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī and al-Jishumī cite desert-tree usage; al-Rāzī calls him the tree bearing faith's fruit; al-Qurṭubī prefers this as gathering the figurative readings. Al-Ālūsī says people were guided to him."}, {"id": "93:7/q03/p16", "position": "He sought or was uncertain about emigration until God guided his departure.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī adds Umm Maʿbad and Surāqa; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ rejects the chronology because emigration followed this early sūra by years."}, {"id": "93:7/q03/p17", "position": "He did not know the heavenly route during the Night Journey and God guided him onward.", "reasons": "Versions say Gabriel left him before the Lote Tree or Throne; al-Rāzī also describes guidance through the heavenly paths."}, {"id": "93:7/q03/p18", "position": "He did not yet know himself or his true identity, and God disclosed it.", "reasons": "Bassām ibn ʿAbd Allāh and parallel reports describe self-recognition, not a change of religion."}, {"id": "93:7/q03/p19", "position": "He lacked worldly livelihood or trade knowledge and God showed him its means.", "reasons": "Abū Muslim connects livelihood to a Prophetic saying on provision through jihad; al-Rāzī says profitable trade attracted Khadīja. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ objects both on chronology and on its inadequacy as the favor intended."}, {"id": "93:7/q03/p20", "position": "He forgot a promised qualification, and God reminded him.", "reasons": "The reports concern the Companions of the Cave, Dhū al-Qarnayn, and the Spirit; 2:282 supplies the forgetting sense of ḍalla."}, {"id": "93:7/q03/p21", "position": "He was powerless and mistreated, until God made him a leader over his people.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī says they would not even accept him as a subordinate before divine strengthening."}, {"id": "93:7/q03/p22", "position": "He did not initially recognize Gabriel at his first appearance, then God enabled recognition.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī adds that the first appearance frightened him."}, {"id": "93:7/q03/p23", "position": "He was separated from the misguided and later guided to mix with and summon them.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī says being 'lost' can mean apart from their religion. Another proposal says he already knew God inwardly but did not publicly oppose his people."}, {"id": "93:7/q03/p24", "position": "As a child he lacked knowledge of God until God created reason, guidance, and knowledge in him.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī distinguishes absence of knowledge at birth from holding a false belief and cites 16:78."}, {"id": "93:7/q03/p25", "position": "Awe on the Night Journey made him forget words of praise, which God then taught him.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī derives the forgetting sense from 2:282 and reports that God taught the admission that the Prophet could not enumerate His praise."}, {"id": "93:7/q03/p26", "position": "He was away from the laws but never spiritually without God's guidance.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says every creature has no intrinsic guidance apart from God's gift, which accompanied the Prophet from the beginning."}, {"id": "93:7/q03/p27", "position": "People called him misguided, although the verse need not endorse their charge.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya records an interpretation in which the community's attribution, rather than an actual religious condition, explains the description."}, {"id": "93:7/q03/p28", "position": "The orphan, lost one, and needy person symbolize missing a teacher, knowledge, and a community, then receiving revelation.", "reasons": "ʿIṣām al-Dīn proposes the linked allegory; al-Ālūsī judges it strained."}]}

Bint al-Shāṭiʾ reports the majority rejection; Elmalılı stresses his reputation for trustworthiness."}, {"id": "93:7/q04/p2", "position": "Prior unbelief is rationally possible in general, but transmitted evidence excludes it here.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī's school requires transmission to decide and even allows rational possibility of later faith and prophethood or removal of prophethood; al-Rāzī's school cites 53:2 to settle this case."}, {"id": "93:7/q04/p3", "position": "A reported Sunni interpretation links the verse to the Prophet's pre-Islamic arrangement of his daughter's marriage.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya transmits Thaʿlab's attribution without developing its argument; the full version repeats it."}, {"id": "93:7/q04/p4", "position": "God protected the young Prophet from intentions to join Meccan entertainments.", "reasons": "ʿAlī's report says he twice intended to join nighttime wedding festivities, slept until sunrise each time, and never again intended evil before revelation."}, {"id": "93:7/q04/p5", "position": "Prior unbelief is rationally impossible because it would repel people from the Prophet.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī attributes this rationale to the Muʿtazila."}, {"id": "93:7/q04/p6", "position": "The extent of pre-prophetic protection from grave indecent sins is disputed.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says strict scholars of his school exempt prophets from them, while the Muʿtazila deny such immunity because reason itself identifies grave wrongs."}]}

Ibn Kathīr quotes 42:52. Al-Ṭabrisī speaks of reason, proofs, and divine favor amid idolatry; Elmalılı emphasizes divine selection and teaching."}, {"id": "93:7/q05/p2", "position": "The verb 'guided' omits its understood object for concision and verse ending rhyme.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī, al-Ālūsī, and Ibn ʿĀshūr derive the object from the second-person pronoun; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ argues the open wording extends to those guided through his mission. Al-Ālūsī objects that the following fa-clauses resist a proposed expansive-generosity account."}, {"id": "93:7/q05/p3", "position": "God guided others through the Prophet and his revealed law.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭāʾ makes him a means of guidance to the lost. Al-Sāmarrāʾī cites 42:52, saying the Prophet too guides to a straight path."}, {"id": "93:7/q05/p4", "position": "This is likely the earliest Qurʾānic use of hadā and resonates with scriptural guidance motifs.", "reasons": "Corpus Coranicum notes biblical and psalmic parallels for personal divine guidance and Syriac dbar as a technical parallel, while listing later Qurʾānic occurrences."}]}
{"id": "93:7/q06", "question": "How is this clause joined grammatically to the preceding question?", "turns_on": "Whether coordination follows the affirmative implication or the earlier negated verb.", "positions": [{"id": "93:7/q06/p1", "position": "It coordinates with the affirmative sense implied by the rhetorical question.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān says a rhetorical question of report is affirmative, allowing an affirmative clause to join it, with parallels 94:1 and 105:2. {"id": "93:7/q07", "question": "What inward meaning is drawn from the Prophet's being lost and guided?", "turns_on": "Which spiritual lack, bewilderment, or transition the inward reading describes.", "positions": [{"id": "93:7/q07/p1", "position": "He sought pure divine love and was guided to gnosis through nearness and affection.", "reasons": "Tustarī and al-Sulamī describe a cup of nearness, knowledge of God's love, and pre-eternal love; Jaʿfar says God made Himself known. Other voices describe longing and ecstatic bewilderment. Al-Najmiyya describes passage from annihilation to sobriety and complete knowledge."}, {"id": "93:7/q07/p2", "position": "He was unaware of his own worth, and God disclosed his noble rank.", "reasons": "Sahl and other voices in al-Sulamī, al-Thaʿlabī, and al-Ālūsī describe unveiling of status and the signs of prophethood."}, {"id": "93:7/q07/p3", "position": "He was bewildered in witnessing divine transcendence, then guided by God to God.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī and al-Najmiyya describe divine bewilderment followed by knowledge or sobriety; al-Wāsiṭī warns ordinary categories of misguidance and guidance do not apply to his supreme rank."}, {"id": "93:7/q07/p4", "position": "The natural self lacked the path to gnosis and was redirected toward knowledge and law.", "reasons": "Tustarī and Sahl describe the soul's poverty; al-Thaʿlabī adds desire as its motive."}, {"id": "93:7/q07/p5", "position": "He moved from inference and conventional forms to direct recognition.", "reasons": "Bandār says divine recognition made proofs and witnesses unnecessary; Ibn ʿAṭāʾ says he was lost from convention, not gnosis."}, {"id": "93:7/q07/p6", "position": "A person's search for their virtue ends when God reveals it.", "reasons": "Al-Sulamī transmits this more general inward application."}]}

{"id": "93:8/q01", "question": "What does 'found you' convey here?", "turns_on": "Whether 'finding' describes an encounter, divine selection, or an inwardly felt reassurance.", "positions": [{"id": "93:8/q01/p1", "position": "God encountered the Prophet in a state of need and aided him.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr treats wajada as 'encountered,' with the needy states as circumstances; the rhetorical question invites the Prophet's assent."}, {"id": "93:8/q01/p2", "position": "Finding conveys God's choosing a rare, precious person.", "reasons": "Elmalılı interprets the repeated 'finding' in the three verses as divine selection (iṣṭifāʾ). Sulamī's Ibn ʿAṭāʾ says finding follows seeking and the Prophet was the sought beloved."}, {"id": "93:8/q01/p3", "position": "The heart verb foregrounds the Prophet's inner reassurance.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ says wajada evokes the Prophet's felt state and psychological consolation amid the remembered favors."}]}
{"id": "93:8/q02", "question": "How does ʿāʾilan describe the Prophet's need?", "turns_on": "Whether the word names material poverty, responsibility for dependents, or spiritual or communal need.", "positions": [{"id": "93:8/q02/p1", "position": "He was poor, needy, or without property.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUbayda/Majāz, Ṭabarī, Farrāʾ, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Qurṭubī, and others cite poetry using yaʿīl/ʿāla for becoming poor; Nāḥḥās and Ibn Qutayba distinguish aʿāla, having dependents. Q 9:28 pairs ʿayla with enrichment; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ notes the Qur'anic pattern. Ibn ʿAmr says Arab resources were scant, although Muhammad remained noble."}, {"id": "93:8/q02/p2", "position": "He had dependents or people whose support fell to him.", "reasons": "Al-Akhfash invokes a Prophetic injunction to begin with those one supports; Māwardī cites a needy traveler in Jarīr's poetry. Rāzī adduces Q 4:3 and 9:28; Qurṭubī cites Q 2:273. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ says dependents can cause poverty. Ālūsī accepts this lexical sense but says Muhammad had no dependents early in life."}, {"id": "93:8/q02/p3", "position": "His need was inward dependence on God, spiritual poverty, or lack of knowledge.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭāʾ and Tustarī describe a poor or yearning soul; Qāshānī describes annihilation of ego; Sulamī's voices variously specify scripture, gnosis's rulings, or proofs. Al-Wāsiṭī warns that ordinary categories of poverty and wealth do not apply to the Prophet in the usual way."}, {"id": "93:8/q02/p4", "position": "The dependents are his community, needy for guidance.", "reasons": "Rāzī says the community depended on him and was poor through ignorance; Elmalılı says needy companions gained through his teaching. ʿIṣām al-Dīn extends the allegory to lacking a teacher and knowledge; Ālūsī calls it strained."}]}
{"id": "93:8/q03", "question": "What readings of ʿāʾilan and its clause are reported?", "turns_on": "The transmitted form and whether the codex variant ends with shelter or enrichment.", "positions": [{"id": "93:8/q03/p1", "position": "The common reading is ʿāʾilan, 'poor or needy,' followed by 'so He enriched.'", "reasons": "Qurṭubī and Abū Ḥayyān identify it as the common or majority reading; Jarīr's verse is cited for the poor person. Jishumī says both readings mean poor."}, {"id": "93:8/q03/p3", "position": "A codex attributed to Ibn Masʿūd or ʿAbd Allāh has ʿadīman, 'destitute,' then 'He enriched.'", "reasons": "Wāḥidī, Rāzī, Bursevī and Ālūsī cite destitute as evidence for material need; al-Aʿmash transmits the wording with enrichment. {"id": "93:8/q04", "question": "How did God enrich the Prophet?", "turns_on": "Whether enrichment denotes worldly resources, contentment, revelation and proof, community support, divine nearness, public recognition, or a response to prayer.", "positions": [{"id": "93:8/q04/p1", "position": "He gave material means, especially Khadīja's wealth.", "reasons": "Thaʿlabī, Wāḥidī, Baghawī, Ṭabrisī, Qurṭubī and others name Khadīja's resources; ʿAṭāʾ says they replaced dependence on Abū Ṭālib. Ibn ʿĀshūr specifies a profit-sharing commercial partnership, and ʿAbduh says he inherited only a camel and maidservant. Reports of famine relief and Abū Bakr's gift add detail."}, {"id": "93:8/q04/p2", "position": "He granted later war spoils and conquered wealth.", "reasons": "Thaʿlabī, Wāḥidī, Baghawī, Ṭabrisī and Biqāʿī append spoils after earlier support; Kashshāf cites the Prophet's report that provision lay beneath his spear. Rāzī and later commentators answer the chronology objection by saying future spoils were certain; Elmalılı relates them to the promise in 93:5. Qushayrī and Ālūsī object that this Meccan sūra preceded warfare."}, {"id": "93:8/q04/p3", "position": "He made the Prophet content, inwardly rich and sufficient with his provision.", "reasons": "Muqātil and al-Farrāʾ identify enrichment with contentment; the latter prefers this over abundance. Ibn ʿAṭiyya includes patience and love of the modest state, with both poverty and wealth beloved; Qushayrī adds receiving before asking. {"id": "96:1/q02", "question": "What is Muhammad commanded to read?", "turns_on": "Whether the omitted object is the Qurʾān, God's name, the phrase itself, or all signs for study.", "positions": [{"id": "96:1/q02/p1", "position": "The Qurʾān being revealed to him.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī explains it as reciting in remembrance of the Creator; Rāzī cites 75:18 and 17:106, while al-Qurṭubī supplies the omitted object as what has been revealed. Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn likewise say the object is omitted; al-Biqāʿī says the Qurʾān comprehends every good. BIQAI: The verb is placed before its prepositional phrase for greater impact, especially as this was the first revelation and reading was the urgent command; its object is omitted to indicate that the reading commanded is the Qurʾān, comprehensive of all good. BIQAI-FULL: Omitting the object of “read” signals that the reading is the comprehensive Qur'an, containing every good; God alone enables the Prophet to read it. BIQAI-FULL: The Qur'an is the healing, clarifying guide to humanity's beginning and end, so the command is to read it reflectively; its description as guidance and mercy reinforces this role.; cites 25:1\n[BIQAI-FULL:v8p480/r4] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Humanity was created in the best form and then reduced to the lowest, producing opposing outcomes by God's prior wisdom and will; He could have guided every soul if He willed. | mentions 95:5, 76:30 ALUSI: The object of iqraʾ is omitted but understood from context as the Qurʾān being revealed; the verb is not intransitive. ALUSI: The command does not impose an impossible task: the Prophet knows that whatever is revealed as Qurʾān is what he is commanded to recite, and the command can include its own wording. ALUSI-FULL: Read has an implied object, what is revealed of the Quran; the verb is not intransitive and باسم ربك is not its object with an extra ba, contrary to Abu Ubayda. ALUSI-FULL: The command is not impossible even if immediate: the Prophet knows that whatever is revealed as Quran is what he must read, so the command itself can be part of the material to read. ALUSI-FULL (الآمدي): Al-Amidi cites the repeated command Read followed by this passage as an example of clarification delayed until after the original command; al-Alusi accepts the passage as the clarification but rejects making the whole passage or basmala the object of the earlier command. ELMALILI: The Prophet's own recitation was the fullest kind, from memory by divine instruction, whether for himself, prayer, teaching others, or dictation. ELMALILI: The command miraculously gave the unlettered Prophet a book to recite, teach, and dictate without writing himself; beginning with the basmala accords with God's lordship. IBNASHUR: The object of “read” is omitted either because the verb is used intransitively to mean begin reading, or because context makes clear that the object is what will be revealed of the Qur'an. IBNASHUR-FULL: The imperative asks for immediate or near-future recitation of words about to be dictated, since no text had previously been read or handed to him. TABATABAI: The apparent sense of iqraʾ is to receive and read what the angel reveals; the command is embedded within the revealed book, like an instruction at a book’s opening. TABATABAI: The wording supports this being the first revelation and implies an omitted object, ‘the Qur’an’ or its equivalent. TABATABAI: The command does not simply use read intransitively with its object omitted, nor does it mean ‘recite to people’ with an omitted complement.; cites 17:106 BINTSHATI: The opening command to recite is striking because it begins revelation to an unlettered Prophet among an unlettered, pagan Bedouin people, with the Book as his miracle. BINTSHATI (الطبري): Al-Tabari did not allegorize the command because its ordinary Arabic meaning, reciting from a written or unwritten text, was clear; Arabs knew rabb as owner and object of worship. BINTSHATI: She prefers the straightforward context: the command to recite is reiterated, and revelation specifies what the Prophet should read in his Lord’s name. ISLAHI-TADABBUR: Qur'an 7:204 and 17:45 show that iqraʾ can mean reciting the Qur'an aloud to an audience; the usage is indicated by these verses.; cites 7:204, 17:45 ISLAHI-TADABBUR: Reciting in the Creator's name presents the Qur'an as God's binding directive, not a preacher's words or a request; people must obey and not mock or trivialize it. ISLAHI-TADABBUR: The Qur'an is uniquely composed entirely of words revealed by God, so its opponents should recognize its exaltedness and fear its wrath."}, {"id": "96:1/q02/p2", "position": "The name of his Lord.", "reasons": "Majāz and Ibn Qutayba read the wording as 'read the name'; Abū ʿUbayda treats bāʾ as extra. Al-Wāḥidī and Rāzī cite al-Akhṭal's poetic construction with bāʾ before sūras. Rāzī objects that the Prophet's 'I am not a reader' would be incoherent and the command redundant. CORPUSCORANICUM (Hirschfeld 1902): Hirschfeld recognizes a correspondence between iqraʾ bi-smi rabbika and the Hebrew formula qārāʾ be-šem YHWH, then proposes proclaim the name of your Lord. ALUSI: The command does not impose an impossible task: the Prophet knows that whatever is revealed as Qurʾān is what he is commanded to recite, and the command can include its own wording.
